context.title: Anti-discrimination laws in US often lack clear wording relevant to multiracial identities
context.snippet:
A new study analyzed US federal and state anti-discrimination laws and found that only one federal law and 22 state laws explicitly include
Anti-discrimination laws in US often lack clear wording relevant to multiracial identities 11.25.26 | PLOS A new analysis highlights the limited appearance of the phrases “perceived race” and “multiracial” in US federal and state anti-discrimination laws, and demonstrates how court cases can be analyzed to explore whether such wording contributes to ambiguity that may hamper equal protection of multiracial people. Victoria Jackson and colleagues at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, US, present these findings in the open access journal PLOS One on November 25, 2026. The number of people who identify as more than one race tripled in the US between 2010 and 2020. Both multiracial people and people of a single race can experience racial discrimination, which may harm physical, mental and economic wellbeing. However, racial discrimination can look different for multiracial people, raising questions about whether anti-discrimination laws adequately protect them. To help establish a framework for addressing these questions, Jackson and colleagues analyzed the wording of US federal and state anti-discrimination laws and explored court records of discrimination cases. The analysis was limited to laws and cases pertaining to criminal justice, education, employment, and housing. Of six federal laws analyzed, only one, pertaining to hate crimes, explicitly includes “perceived race” as a protected class, and none include “multiracial” in their wording. This finding is notable because multiracial people may experience discrimination based on an observer’s inaccurate perception of their race.

context.title: Workers in New York can now see what their bosses say about their job performances
context.snippet:
The new law, effective this week, gives workers the right to see what is inside their personnel files.
Essentially, the idea is to give workers more power to know how their employer is evaluating them. The law is mirrored after Massachusetts legislation, which has had similar protections in place for employees since 2010. The new law also gives the workers the ability to take their case to court, if employers fail to share the documents, Tenenbaum said. “There definitely has been a greater push, holistically, to give employees more rights and to put them on a more equal footing to the employer,” Tenenbaum said. Which employers must follow the new law? The law pertains to all businesses in the state, no matter their industry or size. This means a large corporate company, a government agency, a hospital and a 10-person local business will be held to the same standard under the new law, Tenenbaum said. However, the law only applies to businesses who already have personnel records in place. Employers are not required under the new law to create a new evaluation system for their employees, Tenenbaum said. Which workers will get to see their employee files? Basically anyone who works for an employer who already has a system with personnel records in place. Both current and former employees, full-time and part-time workers are allowed to request their file, according to labor and employment lawyers at Phillips Lytle, a law firm with offices throughout the state. Currently, the law does not specify how long former employees are entitled to their previous files, Phillips Lytle lawyers, James O’Connor and Colleen McMullen, wrote in response to questions.

The regulatory authority for observer identification is 29 CFR § 1602.13, which gives employers two options for acquiring [demographic data](https://legalclarity.org/eeoc-data-collection-requirements-for-employers/): visual surveys of the workforce, or maintenance of post-employment records where state law allows.[6](javascript:void%280%29)eCFR.
A visual survey means that someone in the organization, typically an HR professional or compliance officer, makes a good-faith determination of the employee’s race and ethnicity based on physical appearance observed during normal workplace interactions. The regulation does not prescribe a specific methodology beyond this. There is no required form, no mandatory training certification, and no formal observation protocol in the federal rules. The employer simply selects the category that appears to best fit the individual and records it for the filing.
The classification must use the same federal categories available on the self-identification form.
The second option involves checking existing employment records that may already contain demographic information. Prior job applications, hiring paperwork, and other documents from the onboarding process sometimes include race or ethnicity data that the employee provided in a different context.

octen.title: Employer Beware: New Requirements For Employers With New Hires In Colorado - Employee Rights/ Labour Relations - United States
octen.snippet:
Employers hiring employees in Colorado beware! You may inadvertently commit a hate crime without even knowing it.
The Colorado legislature ended the 2026 regular session by passing a law that makes it a hate crime for an employer, or that employer’s agent, to “demand, confiscate, retain, or otherwise require an individual who is an employee or an applicant for employment or who is performing work or seeking to perform work for the employer in any capacity ... to surrender the individual’s government-issued identification.”
As most U.S. employers know well, federal law imposes an affirmative obligation on employers to verify an applicant’s eligibility to work in the United States when you hire someone. Colorado’s new law doesn’t prevent you from completing such verification, but it does now impose an obligation that you “retain an individual’s government-issued identification only for as long as necessary to verify the individual’s employment eligibility and make a copy of the card.” The law also says that holding onto this identification for “more than ten hours” is always too long.
For most employers, especially those who use E-Verify, compliance with this new requirement isn’t going to be an issue. However, every employer hiring someone in Colorado, including those who never “retain” anyone’s government-issued identification, still needs to take action to ensure compliance with this new law. Specifically, in addition to making sure you don’t “demand, confiscate, retain or otherwise require” someone to “surrender” their government-issued identification, employers must provide notice of this new “hate crime” when verifying employment eligibility.

## Assigned, Not Asked: The U.S. Government’s Written Rules for Sorting Every Worker Into Seven Racial Boxes — and the Training Booklet for HR to Identify Race

10 min read

Aug 23, 2026

--

*An OSINT look at the *EEO-1 report: the “eye-check” procedure written into its instruction booklet, the seven boxes that file Arabs and North Africans as White and Pakistanis alongside the Japanese and Chinese as Asians, and why the resulting named datasets — held in HR* ***and*** *reachable by the government — are an ethnic-targeting risk hiding in plain sight.*

- (EEO repor=Equal Employment Opportunity report by U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission)

Author: Berend Watchus. Independent AI & Cybersecurity Researcher, Trendwatcher. Augus 23, 2026.

### Disclaimer / Editorial Note

This article is analysis and commentary, not an allegation of current wrongdoing. The data-collection program described here — the EEOC’s EEO-1 report and its supporting recordkeeping — is a lawful, decades-old civil-rights mechanism whose stated and original purpose is to *detect and deter* employment discrimination, not to enable it. Nothing here suggests the EEOC, OFCCP, or any employer is presently misusing this data, and the confidentiality protections cited (e.g., Title VII § 709(e)) are real.

The intent of this piece is **prospective risk analysis**. It examines how a system built for a benign purpose creates a durable, named, ethnically-classified dataset — held in HR systems, vendor clouds, and government contractor files — and asks the OSINT question that any such dataset invites: *what could this become useful for, to a future actor with different intentions?* Data collected today for lawful reasons persists, aggregates, and can be repurposed. A named list of individuals and their assigned race is low-risk under a benevolent custodian and high-risk under a hostile one — through breach, leak, FOIA

### Mississippi Discrimination Laws

Federal law makes it illegal for an employer to discriminate on the basis of race, color, age, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, religion, national origin, pregnancy, genetic information (including family medical history), physical or mental disability, military or veteran status, and citizenship or immigration status. Protections for sexual orientation and gender identity stem from federal interpretation of Title VII (following *Bostock v. Clayton County, 2020*), rather than Mississippi state law.

At the state level, Mississippi law provides more limited protections. It does not have comprehensive anti-discrimination protections covering categories such as race, religion, or disability in private employment (these are primarily covered by federal law). Mississippi also does not have separate state-level LGBTQ+ workplace protections.

However, the state does provide some targeted protections. The Mississippi Equal Pay for Equal Work Act (effective July 1, 2022) prohibits sex-based pay discrimination for full-time employees and applies to employers with five or more employees.

**Click here** to read our blog on what acceptable and unacceptable questions to ask during an interview.

### Mississippi Termination Laws
